name: Texas
verdict: Its 340B hospitals cleared $6.5 billion in a year and take an estimated $2.2 billion in tax breaks. No state permit stands between a physician and a new facility. Every July the attorney general gets the list of hospitals that missed the charity care standard. No enforcement action on it has been found.

grade.note: Driver grades I and III follow the Build Brief 2 scale (November 6, 2026). Grades IV and V are provisional Alliance grades, open until the state-grade rubric is published at /methodology/state-grade/.

drivers.label: Section 6001
drivers.title: Physician-owned hospitals
drivers.body: The federal ban applies here as everywhere. Texas has 11 physician-owned hospitals still operating under the grandfather clause, of 55 on the Alliance list. Sixteen more run as joint ventures with health systems; 13 closed and 13 were sold. No new one can open and bill Medicare.
drivers.source: Alliance physician-owned hospital database (research/poh/poh_db_2026-03.json, March 2026): Texas 55 hospitals listed; status Operating 11, Joint Venture 16, Closed 13, Sold/Acquired 13, Under Development 1, Unknown 1

drivers.label: Price Transparency
drivers.title: A state law with small teeth
drivers.body: Texas has its own price-disclosure law, Health and Safety Code chapter 327 (SB 1137, 2021). Hospitals post machine-readable standard charges and a shoppable-services list. SB 331 (2025) limited the chapter to facilities with $10 million or more in gross revenue. The penalty tops out at $1,000 a day for facilities over $100 million. Graded when the rubric is published.
drivers.status: STATE LAW IN FORCE · Rubric pending
drivers.source: Texas Health and Safety Code chapter 327 (tcss.legis.texas.gov, retrieved November 19, 2026): section 327.002 added by Acts 2021, 87th Leg., ch. 1044 (SB 1137), effective September 1, 2021; section 327.0015 ($10 million gross revenue applicability) added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., ch. 1131 (SB 331), section 2, effective June 20, 2025; section 327.008(c) penalties of $100 per violation for facilities with $10 million to $100 million in gross revenue and $1,000 per day above $100 million, as amended by SB 331 section 3

drivers.label: Certificate of Need
drivers.title: No permit to compete
drivers.body: Texas has had no certificate of need law since 1985, when the Texas Health Facilities Commission was abolished. A hospital needs a license under Health and Safety Code chapter 241 and nothing more. A physician can build a surgery center or hospital without a competitor's say.
drivers.linkText: Read the certificate of need desk
drivers.source: Texas Sunset Advisory Commission, Texas Health Facilities Commission agency record (1984-1985 review cycle, 69th Legislature: 'No legislation; agency abolished'); Texas Health and Safety Code chapter 241 (Hospital Licensing Law, no need review); the CON desk's rankings (data/rankings.json: Texas, no CON law, Free Market tier, score 0)

drivers.label: Hospital Subsidies
drivers.title: $2.2 billion a year in tax breaks
drivers.body: Estimated federal income and property tax exemptions for the 166 hospitals in the 340B program with cost reports come to $2.2 billion a year. Against that, $5.0 billion of charity care at cost. Texas has a charity care standard in law. Tax Code 11.1801 ties the exemption to one of four tests. Those hospitals run 2,377 340B child sites and 2,939 contract pharmacy arrangements.
drivers.source: Estimate from CMS hospital cost reports (2023 and 2024 files, latest report per hospital): federal income tax 1,480,945,006 (21% of net income of the 118 profitable hospitals, 7,052,119,075); property tax 729,074,640 on 35,143,113,048 of land, land improvements and buildings at historical cost, at the Lincoln Institute / Minnesota Center for Fiscal Excellence 50-State Property Tax Comparison Study effective commercial rates for taxes paid in 2025 (Houston 2.028% for Harris County hospitals, Fort Stockton 2.087% elsewhere); total 2,210,019,646; no state corporate income tax; charity care at cost 4,952,445,972; Texas Tax Code section 11.1801(a) (four charity care and community benefit standards); HRSA 340B OPAIS export of September 29, 2026 (2,377 child sites, 2,939 arrangements); HB 3708 (89R) reported from House Public Health 7 to 4 on May 1, 2025, died at sine die June 2, 2025
drivers.as_of: exemptions at 2025 rates on hospital fiscal years ending 2023 to 2025

drivers.label: CMS Favoritism
drivers.title: Urban hospitals, rural rules
drivers.body: 21 of the 166 are hospitals in urban areas that CMS treats as rural under 42 CFR 412.103. Memorial Hermann Texas Medical Center, Parkland, Baylor University Medical Center and UTMB are among them. Rural status can lower the 340B eligibility bar for a rural referral center and change Medicare wage-index reclassification. 76 of the 166 are projected to draw Medicare DSH payments in fiscal 2027, with $1.1 billion in uncompensated care payments.
drivers.source: CMS hospital cost reports (Rural Versus Urban = rural) against the CMS FY2027 IPPS final rule impact file, correction notice (urban geographic classification with the Section 401 flag): ASCENSION PROVIDENCE, BAPTIST HOSPITALS OF SOUTHEAST TEXAS DBA BAPTIST BEAUMONT HOSPITAL, BAYLOR UNIVERSITY MEDICAL CTR, CHRISTUS HOSPITAL, CHRISTUS MOTHER FRANCES HOSP-TYLER, CHRISTUS ST MICHAEL, DALLAS COUNTY HOSPITAL DISTRICT dba PARKLAND HEALTH, Dell Seton Medical Center at The University of Texas, GOOD SHEPHERD MEDICAL CENTER, MEDICAL CENTER HOSPITAL , METHODIST HOSPITAL, MIDLAND MEMORIAL HOSPITAL, Memorial Hermann Texas Medical Center, SANTA ROSA HEALTHCARE, SHANNON MEDICAL CENTER, ST. drivers.label: Stark & Anti-Kickback
drivers.title: No room to build rivals
drivers.body: Texas has its own anti-kickback statute. Occupations Code 102.001 makes it a crime to pay or accept anything of value for patient referrals to a licensed practitioner or facility. Section 102.003 carves out whatever federal law allows. Whether Texas self-referral law goes beyond the federal statutes is not yet researched.
drivers.source: Texas Occupations Code chapter 102 (tcss.legis.texas.gov, retrieved November 19, 2026): sections 102.001 (soliciting patients; Class A misdemeanor, third-degree felony on a prior conviction) and 102.003 (federal safe harbors apply); state self-referral review not yet done

agOversight.subtitle: What the office can do, and what it has done

items.title: The charity care standard
items.body: Health and Safety Code 311.045 makes every nonprofit hospital meet one of four charity care standards. The best known is 4 percent of net patient revenue. By July 1 each year the Department of State Health Services sends the attorney general and comptroller the list of hospitals that missed it. By November 1 it sends every hospital's charity care, net patient revenue and tax-exempt benefit figures.
items.source: Texas Health and Safety Code sections 311.045 and 311.0455 (tcss.legis.texas.gov, retrieved November 19, 2026); Tax Code section 11.1801(a)

items.title: Charitable assets
items.body: Property Code 123.002 makes the attorney general a proper party in any proceeding involving a charitable trust, with notice required within 30 days. Business Organizations Code 12.151 to 12.156 let the office examine any Texas entity's books and management. Refusal forfeits the right to do business and is a misdemeanor.
items.source: Texas Property Code sections 123.002 and 123.003; Business Organizations Code sections 12.151, 12.152, 12.153, 12.155 and 12.156 (tcss.legis.texas.gov, retrieved November 19, 2026)

items.title: Hospital sales and conversions
items.body: No Texas statute requires attorney general review of a nonprofit hospital sale, merger or conversion. HB 2747 (2025) would have required notice of material change transactions to the attorney general. It cleared House Public Health 8 to 4 and died in Calendars.
items.source: Texas Legislature Online, HB 2747 (89R) history: filed February 12, 2025; reported favorably as substituted April 28, 2025 (Ayes 8, Nays 4); committee report sent to Calendars May 10, 2025; no further action before sine die June 2, 2025; statute search of the Health and Safety, Business Organizations and Property Codes, November 19, 2026

items.title: Enforcement record
items.body: No attorney general enforcement action on hospital charity care, tax exemption or the 340B program was found. The office's site was searched on October 3 and November 19, 2026.
items.source: texasattorneygeneral.gov site search for hospital charity care, nonprofit hospital and 340B (October 3, 2026, and November 19, 2026): NOT FOUND

rows.title: 340B protection, all comers
rows.body: Would have barred manufacturers, distributors, pharmacy benefit managers and payers from limiting 340B hospitals and their contract pharmacies, with civil penalties. Cleared House Insurance 5 to 2 on April 24, 2025 and died in Calendars.

rows.title: 340B protection, payers only
rows.body: Would have barred health plans, pharmacy benefit managers and other payers from discriminating against 340B entities. Referred to House Insurance April 2, 2025 and never heard.

rows.title: Charity care counted system-wide
rows.body: Would have made a nonprofit system count all its Texas revenue against the charity care standard, and screen patients before billing. Cleared House Public Health 7 to 4 on May 1, 2025 and died.

rows.title: Notice of hospital deals to the attorney general
rows.body: Would have required health care entities to notify the attorney general of material change transactions. Reported from Public Health 8 to 4 and sent to Calendars May 10, 2025.

rows.title: Price transparency, narrowed
rows.body: Limits the state price-disclosure law to facilities with $10 million or more in gross revenue and scales penalties to facility size.
